questions.question: Explain the rule of one man, one claim: who made it, why, and why it was abandoned.
questions.expected_answer: Diggers' committees at the dry diggings in 1870 and 1871 made the rule, later relaxed to two claims, because there was no settled government. Reasons: one digger could only work a small claim of about 9.5 metres square; limiting holdings stopped wealthy men and companies dominating, spread the chance of wealth, and kept the diggings open; diggers from California and Australia knew similar rules. In practice it mainly protected white diggers, and some evaded it by registering claims in others' names. After annexation the government kept it at first, but as mining deepened, reef falls and flooding required costly machinery that only large holders could afford. In 1876 the limit rose to ten claims and later was removed, allowing consolidation, companies and monopoly.

questions.question: Using supply and demand, explain why diamond prices fell in the 1870s and early 1880s.
questions.expected_answer: Price is set where demand meets supply; if supply rises while demand stays the same, price falls. Gem diamonds are valuable because of scarcity and belief. Before 1870 diamonds came in small quantities from India and Brazil; Kimberley soon produced more each year than the world had produced before, so prices fell sharply in the early 1870s. Producers trying to keep income up produced more, for example 3 000 carats at 2 pounds to equal 2 000 carats at 3 pounds, which pushed prices lower: the trap of overproduction. In the early 1880s, companies from the share boom produced as much as possible to pay dividends while a world depression cut demand, so prices fell again and many companies failed. Theft added uncontrolled stones to the market.

questions.question: Describe how De Beers and the Diamond Syndicate controlled the supply and price of diamonds after 1888, and who benefited.
questions.expected_answer: After 1888 De Beers controlled almost all South African mines, so it limited output to what the market would buy at good prices, closed or slowed less profitable workings, cut the workforce and held unsold diamonds in stock. In 1890 it agreed with the London Diamond Syndicate, which bought its output at agreed prices and released stones to cutters and dealers gradually. It worked to buy or bring into agreements new producers such as the Premier Mine. Compounds, searches and IDB laws stopped stolen diamonds reaching the market. Later Oppenheimer, chairman from 1929, built a central selling system. Beneficiaries: De Beers shareholders and directors, London merchants, Antwerp and Amsterdam cutters, Cape revenue. Losers: small diggers, workers whose wages were held down and who lost jobs when output was cut.
